newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram aims to revive insurance bill.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram aims to revive insurance bill.

text.p: India's Finance Minister P.Chidambaram said on Wednesday that the government was forced to withdraw a key insurance bill over policy details, and promised to bring the bill back to parliament.

"It depends on how soon we agree on safeguards (to help Indian industry)," Chidambaram told a group of reporters in his office after the government failed to muster enough support to defeat an amendment proposed by Hindu nationalists.
"Whatever safeguards we take must protect our interests ans at the same time not send the wrong signals abroad," he said.

Earlier, Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral withdrew the Insurance Regulatory Authority of India Bill, to which the major opposition group, the Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) proposed an amendment barring foreign firms.
"The bill only concerns the setting up of a regulatory authority (for the industry)," Chidambaram said.
"Where we got stuck was how do we open it, when do we open it and who we open up to," he said. "BJP is not against opening up to Indians."
"We will come back after resolving this narrow area of difference," Chidambaram told reporters after Gujral's government suffered the embarrassing setback.

The authority to oversee the state-controlled insurance industry was considered an important first step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to private competition, both Indian and foreign, under India's six-year-old economic reforms.
"I thought the BJP would be satisfied with the statement that there is no proposal to allow multinationals and foreign companies in insurance," Chidambaram said.
"My impression until the morning was that they will not press the amendment (to bar foreign companies)," he said. "I...explained it was premature to talk about opening the sector."
The government proposed in its 1997/98 (April-March) budget to open the health insurance sector to a small number of private Indian companies.
Chidambaram said the government was keen not to send the wrong signal to foreign investors, because India's state-run insurance companies already had several joint ventures abroad.
With not enough deputies supporting the bill, Gujral withdrew it rather than suffer defeat.

A Finance Ministry official said Gujral's United Front government, without support from communist allies in the ruling coalition or the BJP, could have pushed the bill through with help from the Congress party, but faced practical problems in assembling a quorum of lawmakers from supporting parties.
The Congress has 140 lawmakers and the BJP and its allies have 194 votes in the 545-member parliament.
Left-wing groups accounting for 52 votes of the United Front's 178 are generally opposed to the liberalisation of insurance.
But Chidambaram said the Communist Party of India (CPI), a member of the Gujral government, had implicity supported the bill. The CPI has 12 lawmakers.
